# Which man is in most danger if the green truck reverses straight backward?

## Short answer

**The bare‑headed man in the orange/red hi‑vis vest, dark T‑shirt and dark shorts — the left‑hand
(nearer) of the two workers standing at the right of the frame, immediately off the truck's tail.**
He is the closest person to the reversing truck's rear, he is the most closely aligned with the
line the truck would travel, and he has his back turned to it. The other man — in the lime‑green
hard hat, orange vest and long dark trousers, holding a rolled‑up drawing — is further back, further
out of the path, and is facing toward the truck.

## Why: the geometry of the scene

**1. Which way is "backward"?** The green PROTRANZ Earthmoving hook‑lift truck is parked broadside
to the camera with its cab, windscreen and front bumper at the LEFT of the frame and its hook‑lift
body, rear axles and rear chassis at the RIGHT. Forward for this truck is therefore to the left of
frame, and **reversing straight backward means it moves to the RIGHT across the picture**, along the
line of its own chassis — straight toward the corner of the frame where the two men are standing.

**2. Everyone at risk is on the right.** Sweeping the rest of the image, there is nobody in front of
the truck, nobody visible in the cab, and nobody alongside it: the only people standing on open
ground are the two men at the right of the frame. (There is a small patch of lime hi‑vis at the
extreme right edge, around the dark tracked machine, but that figure is behind the mesh fence and
shielded by plant, and is farther from the truck's path than either of the two men.)

**3. The near man is the one the truck reaches first.** Measuring from the contact patches of the
truck's four axles and projecting that ground line rearward:

- The rear of the truck's chassis sits at roughly x≈710 px, and the raised hook‑lift arm with its
  J‑hook projects a further ~45 px rearward, to x≈755 px.
- The orange‑vested man's boots are at x≈830–860 px — only about **1–2 m behind the tail of the
  truck**, essentially level with the tip of the protruding hook arm.
- The hard‑hatted man's feet are at x≈890–930 px — roughly **another metre or more further back**.

So along the direction of travel, the orange‑vested man is the first obstacle the reversing truck
would meet.

**4. The near man is also better lined up with the truck's path.** Extrapolating the truck's
near‑side wheel‑contact line (fitted through all four axles) back past the tail and comparing it
with where each man's feet meet the road: both men are standing slightly on the kerb/camera side of
that line, but the orange‑vested man is roughly **a metre closer to it** than the hard‑hatted man is.
A truck of this width reversing hard, with any tail swing or wheels not perfectly straight, sweeps
through exactly the space he occupies; the hard‑hatted man has an extra metre of margin.

**5. He would not see it coming.** He is standing with his back squarely to the camera, facing the
green site fence and the building being demolished — completely absorbed in watching the excavator
work. The truck would come at him from behind and slightly to his left, out of his field of view,
and he is in the truck's rear blind zone. By contrast, the hard‑hatted man is standing in profile,
turned toward the truck, and would almost certainly see it move.

**6. Secondary factors that worsen it for him.** He is wearing no hard hat (just his hair or a soft
cap) and is in shorts and boots, whereas the other man has a hard hat and long trousers. The
hook‑lift arm sticks out rearward at roughly waist/hip height above the road at his position, so
even a short, sharp reverse could spear or sweep him before the chassis itself arrived. The
hard‑hatted man also has a parked dark tracked machine immediately to his right, whereas the near
man stands in open roadway inside the coned‑off zone with nothing to stop or shield the truck.

## Caveats

The two men's feet are at almost the same depth in the image, so the depth estimates above carry
maybe half a metre to a metre of uncertainty, and on a perfectly straight reverse the truck's
near‑side wheels might pass a metre or so beyond both of them rather than over them. That
uncertainty does not change the ranking, though: on every measure — distance to the tail, alignment
with the path, awareness, and protection — the near man is worse off.

One mitigating detail: this is a New Zealand contractor's truck, so it is almost certainly
right‑hand drive, and the side facing the camera (the side the men are on) is the driver's side,
which gives the driver a slightly better mirror view of them. That helps only if the driver looks;
a sudden, rapid reverse gives no time for it, and the man closest to the tail is inside the zone the
mirrors do not cover.

## Conclusion

**The man in the orange hi‑vis vest and shorts, standing with his back turned just off the rear of
the truck (the left one of the pair at the right of frame), is in the most danger of being struck.**
The hard‑hatted man beside him is second, roughly a metre further from the truck's tail and a metre
further out of its path, and facing the right way to see it move.
